meta.title: Connector C: keep it, redesign it, and decide on a sunset with evidence
meta.subtitle: Should Vesper MedTech discontinue sterile connector C and redeploy the team to connector D?
meta.purpose: Decide on the CEO's proposal to discontinue connector C, February 2027 board
meta.confidentiality: Board discussion document. Synthetic benchmark data

inputs.label: Choices made without the user (unavailable)
inputs.content: Mode deck_detailed; audience board deciding on the CEO's exit proposal; theme navy; storyline approved as drafted

storyline.governing_thought: Keep connector C and redesign it: exit in 2027 would cost $4.75M–5.5M in year one and break the board's cash and bundle limits

exec_summary.text: C's 8.3% reported margin is an allocation effect; on direct contribution it is Vesper's most profitable connector

sub_points.text: Only $0.4M of the $3.3M charged to C would go with it
C earns 63% direct contribution margin, against 50% for D

exec_summary.text: Exit would cost $5.5M in year one and $3.4M a year after, and it breaks the cash and bundle limits

sub_points.text: Moving C customers to D wins back at most $750K a year
Penalties of $2.1M are 2.3 times the 2027 cash limit

exec_summary.text: The case against C is not proven: the renewal gap reflects who buys C, and the service gap is in bundles

sub_points.text: C buyers are smaller, older-equipment, lower-coverage accounts
Bundle fill is 91% against 95% required; the dashboard hides it

exec_summary.text: Redesign C now, renew both bundles with 2029 exit terms, and decide on a sunset in 2028

sub_points.text: Redesign alone adds contribution within the cash limit
It pays back in a year if savings reach 44% of the estimate

next_steps.action: Reject the Q2 2027 exit and approve the $550K C redesign, with line conversion gated on the two-site pilot
Renew both bundle agreements with C included and notice terms that allow a 2029 exit
Report fill by bundle and recover the nine bundle customers to the 95% minimum
Run the two-site pilot and report measured savings and requalification needs
Validate the D adapter with C accounts and bring the sunset decision back with acceptance data

sections.title: What the evidence against C shows

lead_message.text: Connector C looks unprofitable because of shared overhead: 88% of its allocated cost would stay with Vesper after an exit

bullets: **Direct variable cost:** fully avoidable; it ends with the last C shipment
**Avoidable fixed cost:** Finance's estimate of what retiring the SKU would really remove
**Shared cost that stays:** regulatory documentation and plant depreciation, spread by historical engineering hours

lead_message.text: Exit would cut first-year contribution by $5.5M, and moving C customers to D would win back at most $750K a year

**Migration to D:** a ceiling from three sales interviews, and only where adapters and qualification are complete
**Best case:** a loss of $4.75M in year one and $2.65M a year after, even if the full 25% moves to D

lead_message.text: The renewal gap of 9 percentage points shows who buys C; it does not prove that C drives customers away

slides.rationale: Claim, confounders and the missing test side by side -> text columns

columns.header: The claim rests on a snapshot, not a test
detail: The CEO's scatter plot compares hospital renewal rates by product mix
It shows that C accounts renew less often, not why
No account in the sample is seen before and after a change in C

columns.header: C buyers differ in ways that predict churn on their own
detail: C is concentrated in accounts running legacy equipment
C accounts get lower customer-success coverage
Each of these can lower renewal whether or not C is in the order

columns.header: Before acting on it, test it like for like
detail: Compare C and non-C accounts of the same size, equipment and coverage
Track renewal where coverage rises but C stays
Until then, read the gap as a coverage signal, not a product verdict
The evidence neither proves nor rules out a C effect

footnotes: Renewal comparison from the CEO's scatter plot of hospital renewal rates by product mix; no account-level data in the pack

**Exit does not fix it:** without C, bundles that specify C cannot be filled at all

sources.name: Team analysis of the briefing pack

constraints.item: 95% contracted bundle fill rate (nine of fourteen major relationships bundle C)
constraints.effect: already breached at 91%; exit would make the bundles impossible to fill, so the plan fixes bundle fill under every option

constraints.item: $0.9M one-time cash approved for 2027 portfolio changes
constraints.effect: exit penalties of $2.1M are 2.3 times the limit; redesign at $550K fits but leaves $350K for uncosted requalification and bundle fixes

constraints.item: $2.1M first-year bundle penalties, one-time not recurring
constraints.effect: counted once in the first-year effect and dropped from the recurring loss

constraints.item: D spare capacity of $1.5M revenue and customer-specific adapter validation
constraints.effect: caps migration benefit at $750K a year; treated as best case, not base case

constraints.item: Two bundle agreements under renewal now
constraints.effect: renewals must keep 2029 exit terms or the sunset option disappears

constraints.item: Four-month validation and possible requalification at two customers
constraints.effect: payback stated from project start (about 9.3 months) and requalification flagged as excluded cost

constraints.item: Opportunity cost of the design team's four months on C instead of D
constraints.effect: not quantified in the pack; stated as an open unknown rather than invented

alternatives.option: Orderly 2029 sunset with no redesign, team moves to D now
alternatives.why: avoids penalties and cash, but forgoes up to $1.25M a year of savings for $550K; D's gain is capped by its $1.5M spare capacity; kept as the 2028 decision

alternatives.option: Exit now and migrate customers to D
alternatives.why: loses $5.5M in year one ($4.75M best case) and $2.65M–3.4M a year after; replacement needs $6.8M of D sales

alternatives.option: Partial exit for non-bundle C customers
alternatives.why: pack has no customer-level split; would give up C's 63% contribution margin while most fixed cost stays

failure_threshold.threshold: below 44% of the $1.25M estimate (about $550K a year) the redesign no longer recovers its cost within one year of savings
failure_threshold.range: exit first-year effect −$5.5M base / −$4.75M best case; recurring −$3.4M / −$2.65M; redesign payback 5.3 months after validation at full estimate

consistency.headline: Keep connector C and redesign it: exit in 2027 would cost $4.75M–5.5M in year one and break the board's cash and bundle limits
consistency.fix: Migration to D shown as best case only; renewal gap described as not proven rather than disproven; payback quoted from project start
